projects.name: Road Runner
projects.thesis: Most websites collect leads. This one queries the business behind it.
projects.summary: Road Runner is the connective layer between a company's front door and its systems of record. The website stops being a brochure and becomes an interface to the CRM, the inventory database, and the finance system — in both directions.
points: One inquiry form, many audiences: the form asks who you are and branches — a homeowner asks for samples, a builder wants trade terms, an architect wants specification data.

Relationship resolution: name the company you're working with and it is matched against the CRM, the record is linked, and the existing commercial relationship — including transaction volume from the finance system — comes with it.
Live data as an experience: stock, lead times, availability and pricing answered on the page instead of 'someone will get back to you'.
Landing pages and campaigns in minutes, with UTM tagging carried end to end so engagement lands back on the same record.
The CRM revamp is a by-product: branching logic forces a real taxonomy of who you sell to, so the CRM ends up shaped like the business rather than like the software's defaults.

case.problem: A company's systems each know something the customer needs, and none of them can be reached from the only place the customer actually goes. The CRM knows the account, the inventory system knows the stock, the finance system knows the trading history — and the website, the front door, knows none of it. So every enquiry starts from zero, is answered by a human reading three screens, and arrives in the CRM as an orphan lead with no relationship attached.
built: A front door that identifies the visitor and branches — one entry point, a genuinely different engagement per audience.
Company-name resolution against the CRM, so an enquiry attaches to the account that will fulfil it instead of creating another duplicate.
A read layer into inventory and finance, so stock, lead times and account-tier pricing can be answered on the page.
Per-client and per-campaign landing pages with UTM tagging carried end to end, so engagement lands back on the same record.
Reporting built on the unified record rather than on each silo's own version of the truth.
changed: 170 per-client landing pages live and tracked, up from 150 three weeks earlier — each one generated in minutes rather than queued behind a developer.
229 stonemasons mapped to the businesses they actually work with. Before the reach view existed, only 20 had any recorded relationship at all.
Enquiries arrive segmented, attributed and attached to an account, so the qualification happens before a human reads them.
The CRM ends up restructured as a by-product: branching logic forces a real taxonomy of who the business sells to.
Built in 109 hours across May and June 2026, site and platform together.

projects.name: Kervio
projects.thesis: An AI-first quoting-to-manufacturing platform for stone fabrication.
projects.summary: Conceived, specified and built with Australian stone fabricators: the quote-to-manufacture workflow of a shop, as software. Product architecture, pricing model and roadmap defined personally; built by directing AI engineering agents under a disciplined human-in-the-loop method.
points: Architecture, pricing model (per-seat / per-quote / per-shop) and roadmap authored, not outsourced.
Live multi-tenant production system with real fabricators, not a prototype.
A repeatable method for directing AI to build complex vertical software: specification, acceptance criteria, ground-truth verification gates.
Geometry and vision components carried through a provisional-patent workstream with counsel.

case.problem: Stone fabrication shops quote from spreadsheets and drawings, then re-enter the same job into manufacturing. The quote and the cut are two different documents maintained by two different people, and the margin leaks in the gap between them. Nothing on the market was built for how these shops actually work, because the shops are too small for enterprise software and the workflow is too specific for generic tools.
built: A quoting-to-manufacturing workflow modelled on how fabricators actually run a job, developed with Australian shops rather than for them.
Product architecture, pricing model (per-seat / per-quote / per-shop) and roadmap authored personally.
A live multi-tenant production system, built by directing AI engineering agents under specification, acceptance criteria and ground-truth verification gates.
Geometry and vision components carried through a provisional-patent workstream with counsel.
changed: The quote becomes the manufacturing instruction — one document, not two.
Proof that the method scales: complex vertical software, built and commercialised without an engineering team.

images.caption: The quote is the manufacturing instruction. Every edge carries its profile, finish and exposure; mitre joins and cutouts are specified here and flow straight through to pricing and the cut list.
images.alt: Kervio piece configurator showing an L-shaped benchtop with edge profiles and dimensions

projects.name: Alpha Surfaces inquiry engine
projects.thesis: One form. Four audiences. Four completely different conversations.
projects.summary: A single inquiry form on a stone supplier's website that identifies whether the visitor is a homeowner, stonemason, architect or builder, and runs a different engagement for each — including resolving the partner company they name against the CRM.
points: Self-segmenting form: the visitor tells you what they are, and the form reconfigures around them.
Company-name lookup against the CRM, linking the inquiry to the existing account rather than creating another orphan lead.
Sample requests, specification packs and trade paths as separate journeys off one entry point.
The commercial payoff: an inquiry arrives already segmented, already attributed, already attached to the account that will fulfil it.

case.problem: A stone supplier's website had one contact form for four completely different customers. A homeowner wanting a sample, a stonemason checking stock, an architect needing specification data and a builder chasing lead times all arrived as the same undifferentiated enquiry, into the same inbox, to be sorted by hand. The account relationships that already existed in the CRM were invisible at the moment they mattered most.
built: A self-segmenting enquiry path: the visitor declares what they are and the form reconfigures around them.
Company-name lookup against the CRM at the point of enquiry, linking to the existing account and its trading history.
Four distinct journeys — sample requests, trade pricing, specification packs, lead-time answers — off a single entry point.
Routing rules that send each type to the right team with the right priority.
changed: 3,025 organisations sit behind the company lookup, so an enquiry attaches to the account that will fulfil it instead of creating another orphan lead.
Enquiries arrive pre-sorted by audience and routed to the right team with the right priority.
The specification path makes architect interest visible months before the order it eventually produces.

unity.name: Data unity
unity.bad: Your systems each hold a different version of the same customer. Every report is an argument.
unity.ok: Mostly one version of the truth, with known gaps at the edges.

routing.name: Speed to response
routing.bad: Enquiries cool off before anyone touches them. This is the cheapest money on the table.
routing.ok: Enquiries reach someone fast; the refinement is scoring and prioritisation.

frontdoor.name: Front-door intelligence
frontdoor.bad: Your website treats a first-time browser and a $200k account exactly the same.
frontdoor.ok: The site knows something about who's there — the next step is letting it answer questions.

attrib.name: Attribution
attrib.bad: You are spending without knowing what works, which means you're guessing about the next spend.
attrib.ok: You can trace most revenue to a source; the gap is tying it through to closed value.

speed.name: Speed to launch
speed.bad: Campaign ideas die waiting for a page. Marketing moves at the speed of your dev queue.
speed.ok: You can move quickly; the win is templating it so anyone can.

owner.name: Ownership
owner.bad: No one owns the revenue system, so it degrades quietly between fires.
owner.ok: There is an owner — the question is whether they have the leverage to build, not just maintain.

unity.d: One canonical customer object, with finance and ops joined to it. Everything else in this list depends on this being done first.

routing.t: Route on signal, not on rota
routing.d: Score inbound on fit and intent, assign it in seconds, and alert on the accounts that matter. Fastest measurable win, usually inside two weeks.

frontdoor.d: A self-segmenting enquiry path that asks who the visitor is, resolves their company against the CRM, and answers live questions from your data.

attrib.d: UTM discipline end to end, carried through the CRM to closed revenue, so spend decisions stop being folklore.

speed.d: A per-campaign, per-client landing page system anyone can run — tagged, tracked and reporting back into the same record.

owner.d: Not a full-time hire. A senior operator with a defined remit and a build backlog, working a set number of hours a month.

outcomes.d: Full teardown of CRM, data model, process and reporting, with a sequenced fix list you own.

numbers.label: Before the seven questions, one
numbers.head: What is the number you want moved?
numbers.lead: Pick one and I will tell you what it usually turns out to be, roughly what it costs to fix, and what I would need from you to start. No email required to read the answer.

items.read: Almost never a speed problem. It is a routing problem — the enquiry lands somewhere nobody owns, and the clock starts before anyone has been told. The fix is ownership at the moment of arrival: every inbound routed to a named person inside a minute, with an escalation if they do not touch it.
items.need: Read access to the CRM and one week of raw enquiries, unfiltered.

items.read: Before adding sources, I would find out what the current ones are actually worth. Most companies I see are paying for three channels and closing from one, and cannot prove which. More volume on top of that just makes the misallocation more expensive.
items.need: Twelve months of closed-won and closed-lost with the source attached, however messy.

items.read: A single conversion rate is usually hiding two populations moving in opposite directions. Split it by source and segment first and the number often stops being a problem and starts being a decision about which segment to stop serving.
items.need: Opportunity history with stage timestamps. Stage names can be a mess; I will map them.

items.read: Nearly always the wrong number to optimise. Cheap leads that never close are more expensive than dear ones that do. I would rebuild this as cost per closed-won by channel, which usually reorders the whole spend and occasionally kills someone's favourite campaign.
items.need: Ad spend by channel and the CRM's source field, even if it is 40% blank.

items.read: The honest question is how many hours a week your reps spend on things that are not selling. In the teams I have measured it is between eleven and nineteen. Most of it is data entry, quoting and chasing information that already exists somewhere in the business.
items.need: An hour with two reps, screen shared, doing their actual admin. Not a survey.

items.read: This is the one I have built twice. If the price depends on configuration, someone senior is being asked to do arithmetic, and the delay is entirely the queue in front of them. Push the rules into software and quoting stops being a role.
items.need: Twenty recent quotes and thirty minutes with whoever currently prices the hard ones.

numbers.after: That is the written answer. The useful one needs about ten minutes and two questions about your business.

ask.head: The questions you would ask on a call.
ask.lead: The common ones have answers Sean wrote himself. Ask something else and the page will assemble one from everything he has written about his work — and tell you which kind of answer you are reading.

bank.q: What would you do in the first month?
bank.a: Week one is read-only: your CRM, your enquiry log, a week of calls, and an hour each with two reps doing their actual admin. Week two you get the map and the three things I would fix, sequenced, with hours against each. Nothing gets built until you have seen both and disagreed with at least one of them.

bank.q: How do you engage with companies?
bank.a: Monthly blocks of hours, no minimum term, no retainer that buys you nothing. The first block is diagnostic and ends in something live, so you find out early whether this is working. Twenty hours a month is the common shape. I hold two engagements at a time and I hand over the source, because the point is that you stop needing me — an arrangement that depends on you never learning how it works is not one I would sign either.

$200 an hour, bought in monthly blocks. Twenty hours a month is the common shape — that is $4,000 and it is roughly a third of what the equivalent full-time hire costs once you load it. There is no retainer that buys you nothing, no minimum term, and the scope builder further down this page will price your actual list without you speaking to me.

Agencies are structurally good at campaigns and structurally bad at systems, because a system needs someone who will still be there in month nine. Most of what gets sold as revenue operations is a deck and a Notion board. I hand over working software in your stack, with the source, and the whole point is that you stop needing me.

Usually within a fortnight, sometimes the same week if the first block is diagnostic rather than build. I hold two engagements at a time; a third is where the quality goes. If I cannot start when you need me I will say so rather than book you in and stretch it.

The first block is deliberately small and ends in something live, so you find out in weeks rather than quarters. If the diagnosis is wrong you have spent twenty hours and you own the analysis anyway. I would rather lose the engagement in week two than defend it in month six.

bank.q: Do you write the code yourself?
bank.a: Yes, directed through AI — which is the reason the economics work at all. Twenty-five years of knowing what the system should do, and a method for turning that judgement into working software in days. Kervio and Road Runner were both built this way, by me, and both are running in production. The work section on this page is the evidence.

bank.q: What size company do you work with?
bank.a: Companies with real revenue and no revenue operations function — usually somewhere between $2M and $50M, ten to a hundred and fifty people. Below that there is not enough process to be worth systematising. Above it you should be hiring the function, and I am happy to tell you that on the call.

bank.q: Do I have to change CRM?
bank.a: Almost never, and I will push back hard if someone suggests it. A migration is nine months of pain that solves a problem you usually do not have. Nearly every CRM I have seen is fine; what is broken is what does and does not reach it.

bank.q: What are you not good at?
bank.a: Brand, creative and paid media buying — I can tell you whether a channel pays, not how to make the ad better. Anything that needs a large team held together over years; I am the wrong shape for that and it is why I work in blocks. And I am slow to be diplomatic about a number that is being reported in a way I think is misleading.

San Francisco, having built commercial systems across the US, Australia and Asia. Most of the work is remote and asynchronous by design — the artefacts are the software and the analysis, not the meetings — but I will come and sit with a sales team for the diagnostic week if it is the difference between guessing and knowing.

tiers.label: Where this sits
tiers.head: What you are looking at is the entry level.
tiers.lead: This page is the smallest useful version of the thing: one front door, instrumented, deciding in the browser. It is the base engagement, it goes live in weeks, and it is deliberately the cheapest thing on this list. It is not the product. It is the first tier of one.

items.w: What is running on this page
items.d: Identity resolution at the account level, behavioural scoring you can interrogate, a stage and a next action, and an event stream shaped as CRM events from the first line. Live in two to three weeks on your existing stack, with the source handed over.

The same events, pointed at the platform instead of at a panel. Road Runner is the connective layer between the front door and the systems that actually hold your business — CRM, ERP, stock, pricing, delivery. It answers the visitor's question from your live data, writes the record, routes the account to a named owner and tells them what to say. That is the difference between a page that watches and a system that acts.
items.note: Where most of the value is. 60–120 hours.

items.w: When the shape is yours, not mine
items.d: Configured quoting, brokered pricing, capacity and scheduling, dealer and franchise portals, whatever the business actually runs on. Kervio is one of these built end to end for stone fabrication. This is where the engagement stops looking like marketing technology and starts looking like the operating system of the company.
items.note: Scoped from the diagnostic, not from a price list.

tiers.foot: The tracking on this page is the demonstration, not the offer. Nobody has ever bought analytics from me; they buy the layer above it, and this is the cheapest honest way to show you what that layer does.
